cues.text: One room, a whole family
Cristiano Ronaldo was born in 1985 in Funchal, on the Portuguese island of Madeira.
His family was poor.
He shared one bedroom with his brother, Hugo, and his sisters, Elma and Kátia.
Open the window of the little house.
His mother, Dolores, worked as a cook and a cleaner.
His father, José, was a gardener, and helped look after the kit at a local club, Andorinha.
That is where Cristiano started playing, when he was seven.
You don’t need a lot of things to have a big dream. Your family can be your first team.
Across the sea at twelve
In 1997, when Cristiano was twelve, the big club Sporting, in Lisbon, gave him a three-day trial, and then signed him.
He had to leave Madeira and his family behind, and move across the sea to Lisbon.
Sail the boat to Lisbon.
Moving so far from home at twelve would be hard for anyone.
At his new school he was popular, but he found schoolwork difficult.
Once he lost his temper with a teacher, and he had to leave that school.
Being new somewhere is hard. It’s okay to miss home, and to ask a grown-up for help.
A racing heart
When Cristiano was fifteen, doctors found a problem with his heart.
Sometimes it beat much too fast.
The problem was serious enough that it could have stopped him playing football.
Slow the racing heart.
The club told his mother, Dolores, and she agreed that he should go to hospital.
Doctors fixed the problem with a laser, in an operation on his heart.
He went home the same day, and a few days later he was training again.
If something feels wrong in your body, tell a grown-up. Asking for help is brave.
Missing his dad
In 2003, at eighteen, Cristiano moved to Manchester United in England.
Later he called his manager there, Alex Ferguson, his father in sport.
But in 2005, when Cristiano was twenty, his own father, José, died after a long illness.
José had been the kit man at Cristiano’s very first club.
Lift the photo frame to remember him.
Losing a parent is one of the saddest things that can happen, and feeling better can take a long time.
Grief can feel heavy. Talk about the people you miss, and let others care for you.
Booed, but not beaten
At the 2006 World Cup, Portugal played England.
After an incident involving Cristiano, his Manchester United teammate Wayne Rooney was sent off.
Back in England, crowds booed Cristiano all through the next season.
He asked to leave the club, but United said no.
Turn the boos into cheers.
Cristiano kept playing his best.
That season he scored twenty league goals for the first time, and Manchester United won the Premier League.
When people are unkind, you don’t have to believe them. Keep doing your best.
Carried by his team
In 2004, when Cristiano was nineteen, Portugal lost the final of the European Championship to Greece.
Twelve years later, at Euro 2016, he was Portugal’s captain in the final against France.
But he was taken off after twenty-five minutes.
Lift the trophy.
His teammates kept going, and Portugal won their first ever major trophy.
In Madeira, the airport was renamed after him.
Years earlier, he had given money to the hospital that saved his mother’s life, to build a cancer centre.
Your team can carry you when you can’t go on. Later, you can help carry others.
